title: Runtime helpers for function-call contract validation and ergonomic invocation
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Context: We need a small, consistent runtime layer across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs that performs function/schema validation and provides ergonomic invocation helpers for function/tool calling. This ticket bundles the cross-language runtime contracts, example patterns, retry semantics for function invocations, streaming-friendly invocation flows, and migration notes for existing SDK consumers.

Goals:
- Provide a lightweight runtime validator that checks incoming function definitions (name, params schema, required/optional fields, enums) and outgoing invocation payloads to prevent runtime panics and unexpected RPCs.
- Offer language-idiomatic invocation helpers that: validate arguments, marshal to the wire format, surface structured errors, and integrate with streaming responses and token-level partial results.
- Define and implement retry and idempotency semantics for function invocations (exponential backoff, jitter, idempotency keys for side-effectful tools).
- Deliver examples and recipes for Python/TS/Go showing best practices: synchronous calls, async/await patterns, streaming/resume, and batched invocation scenarios.
- Ensure minimal runtime overhead and clear guidance for opt-out (zero-cost validation via codegen or compile-time types when available).

Design decisions and trade-offs considered:
1) Runtime vs compile-time validation: Provide both. Runtime validator for hosted scenarios and dynamic schemas. Encourage codegen/typegen for strongly-typed apps to avoid runtime checks.
2) Deep structural validation: Support JSON Schema subset (types, required, enums, min/max length, pattern). Avoid full JSON Schema complexity to reduce bundle size.
3) Streaming ergonomics: Invocation helpers must support partial function call replies (e.g., function returns a stream of events or incremental JSON patches). We'll expose a streaming iterator in Python/Go and an async async-iterator/Observable-like object in TS.
4) Retries and idempotency: For non-idempotent functions, default to no automatic retry. For idempotent pure queries, apply bounded retry policy with exponential backoff and jitter. Provide helper to attach idempotency tokens to invocation metadata.
5) Error shaping: Create a normalized error envelope with fields: code, phase (validation|transport|function), message, schema_errors (if validation failed), and suggestion links. This helps the Console and SDKs map errors to UX states.

Planned API surfaces (high level):
- validateFunctionSchema(schema: object | string): ValidationResult  // runtime check with detailed errors
- buildInvocationPayload(functionName: string, args: object, opts?): {payload, idempotencyToken}
- invokeFunction(client, invocationPayload, {streaming: boolean, retryPolicy?, timeout?}) => invocation result or async iterator
- attachTelemetry(invocation, meta) // internal hook for metrics/tokens/cost breakdowns

Language-specific notes:
- Python: sync and async helpers. Provide context manager for streaming invocations to ensure proper cancellation and KV cache handling. Keep dependency footprint small. Use pydantic-lite validator for runtime checks or generated dataclasses alternative.
- TypeScript: Offer both runtime validators (lightweight) and generated TS types via codegen. Streaming will return an AsyncIterable that yields typed partial results. Keep browser bundle size < 10KB for runtime validator.
- Go: Provide compile-time-friendly interfaces and a small runtime validator for dynamic cases. Streaming uses channels; provide helper wrappers to simplify goroutine lifecycles and error propagation.

Acceptance criteria:
- Cross-language runtime validator implemented with identical validation rules and error shape in Python/TS/Go.
- Invocation helpers for sync/async/streaming implemented and covered by unit + integration tests.
- Retry semantics documented and available as configurable policies; idempotency token helper exists.
- Examples for Python, TS, and Go in the SDK repos and a short Guide in the Console docs.
- Performance: runtime validation adds <5% latency to cold invocations and negligible CPU for hot paths.
- Security review completed for function invocation surface (code executed as a result of function calls, metadata handling).

Testing plan:
- Unit tests exercise validator edge cases (required fields missing, type mismatches, enum violations, pattern failures).
- Integration tests simulate streaming function responses and ensure streaming helpers correctly yield partial events and handle cancellation.
- Fault injection tests for retry: simulate transient network failures and ensure retry policy only applies when safe.
- Property-test generated schemas to ensure validator is robust against unexpected shapes.

Migration and rollout plan:
1) Implement runtime validators and helpers behind an opt-in flag in early SDK releases.
2) Publish examples and a migration guide describing opt-in and codegen alternatives.
3) Start a Beta program with a handful of internal teams and close customers.
4) After metrics review and security sign-off, flip the opt-in to default "on" in the next minor SDK release and add telemetry to measure any regressions.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Exact JSON Schema subset we accept (list to finalize with research).
- Do we provide server-side validation hooks or only client-side? (server-side makes console/hosted API more robust but requires API changes).
- Default retry policy parameters for idempotent invocations.

References and artifacts:
- Design doc (placeholder): drive.redwood.ai/docs/sdk-fn-call-runtime-design (internal).
- Example PR skeleton: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-python/pull/XXXXX (will link when created).

Notes: This ticket intentionally focuses on runtime helpers and ergonomics rather than full codegen pipelines. Codegen/typegen integration will be tracked in a follow-up ticket once the runtime contract stabilizes.
